items.title: Louie Bellson — Smithsonian Jazz Oral History
items.q: Then I did the one with Billy Cobham, where it’s titled, When Cobham Meets Bellson. We did those in Europe.

ctx.x: Let’s talk about other younger drummers, then. You were talking about drummers. I’ve got an LP here called The Matterhorn: the Louie Bellson Drum Explosion. You’ve got two drum sets on the cover. The liner notes describe the project. The other drummer’s always referred to as “the other drummer.” But when one puts it on – if Ken or I or you put it on, we can tell who that other drummer is.
Right. So can you talk about this project and why he never go mentioned?

items.title: Louie Bellson interviewed by Monk Rowe, Sarasota, Florida, April 12, 1996
items.q: But I think Ray said it, he said “well if you drew the plans in ‘38 then you’re the first one.” Because what I did, I just did a thing with just the two bass drums, but you came out with a whole set, the whole thing, see? So the players that followed me on that were Eddie Shaughnessy and the Sam Woo

ctx.x: Oh — a drummer knows that, yes.

Well a lot of the young drummers, well some of the older guys like Tiny Kahn was a great orchestrator, great arranger. And today, Billy Cobham, Steve Gadd, Tony Williams, a lot of these guys are composing and writing, and Harvey Mason, drummers like that you know, not only great percussion players but they’re very sensitive as to what the music is all about.
And when was it that you really felt that you could become a professional musician?
